In eCommerce, a great deal of attention usually goes to the storefront: product pages, filters, offers, price, availability, logistics. None of that is going away. But if more and more comparison and preliminary selection are handled by AI agents, then in the DACH context another layer becomes especially important: how exactly the store or supplier is represented for machine reading, and where mere data ends and verifiable trust begins.

- In product-based scenarios, the agent already works well with price, availability, specifications, and delivery time. This means that catalog transparency by itself does not create a durable differentiator. Moreover, if a store is structurally distinguishable only in terms of commoditized attributes, the system will reduce it even faster to a standard offer comparison. Economically, this increases margin pressure and weakens everything that has not been translated into verifiable signals.
- That is why the more interesting question is not “how can we make the feed even easier to deliver,” but rather “which elements of non-price value can be anchored architecturally.” Product origin, supply chain, certification, authorized partner status, liability terms, demonstrable specialization — these are no longer just description fields. In an agent-based environment, such elements can become the boundary between a faceless listing and a supplier whose attributes cannot be reduced to price.
- In DACH, another layer is added here: data minimization and careful handling of consent. In theory, agent-based scenarios make it possible to respond with parameterized facts without immediately transferring the full user profile. If this proves practically workable, then the local regulatory culture may turn out to be not an obstacle, but a factor in the maturity of digital infrastructure.

What do you think: in DACH eCommerce, will the first competitive layer for agent-based scenarios be price and logistics, or precisely verifiable origin and accountability?
